o: In a tree, starting anywhere, collect every coin (coins within distance 2 of your position are picked up automatically) and return to the start, minimizing traversed edges. Any walk visiting a set of vertices and returning costs 2 · (edges of the Steiner subtree spanning those vertices). Distance-2 collection means we never need to visit a coin's vertex nor its neighbor: so repeatedly prune coin-less leaves, then prune two more layers of leaves; whatever remains must be walked, costing 2·(|V′|−1) (0 if ≤1 vertex remains). Example 1 prunes 0,1 and 5,4, then two more layers leave {2,3} → cost 2.
k: The answer is twice the edge count of the minimal subtree that must be entered.
Coin-less leaves are useless — peel them topologically (like leaf-pruning).
Because collection reaches distance 2, peel two additional leaf layers regardless of coins.

a.i: Simulate pruning with degrees: first repeatedly remove degree-1 vertices without coins (their subtrees hold nothing useful). Then remove the current leaf layer twice, since standing two steps away collects those coins. The surviving induced subtree is exactly what a tour must cover.
s: Build adjacency and degrees; queue all coin-less leaves.
Pop leaves, mark dead, decrement neighbors, enqueue newly coin-less leaves.
Repeat twice: remove all current alive vertices with degree ≤ 1.
a.t: O(n) — each vertex is peeled once per phase

w: This peeling technique generalizes 'minimum subtree spanning required vertices with radius r tolerance'. Pitfalls: handling n = 1 (answer 0), trees with a single coin (peeling may empty everything), and remembering that the final two layers peel regardless of coins. Follow-up: distance-3 collection (peel three layers), or returning the actual walk.
